e.t: This word is a personal name, referring to “Nebuzaradan.” It identifies the same individual throughout its Hebrew Old Testament occurrences rather than describing an object, action, or quality. The name appears 16 times in 15 verses, concentrated in 2 Kings and Jeremiah. Its precise role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions as a person’s name. The biblical text repeatedly places this named person within accounts involving the king of Babylon and events surrounding Jerusalem’s fall.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “enchantment,” naming a practice associated with seeking or using supernatural signs or powers. Its meaning is presented through its use in Numbers, where it appears twice in the Old Testament corpus. In both occurrences, the word is connected with speech about Israel and with attempts to discern or affect what would happen to them. The surrounding verses are needed to explain the precise force in each passage, but the central idea is enchantment rather than ordinary speech or observation.

gl: a collection , i.e. community of persons
d: a collection , i.e. community of persons

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to a people group or nation—a gathered population viewed as a distinct community. It can describe nations broadly, or people as a collective body. In the Old Testament, this word occurs three times, with English renderings “nations” and “people.” Its use reaches from the description of peoples in Genesis and Numbers to a call for the nations to praise the LORD in Psalm 117. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on a particular people or on nations generally.

This Hebrew word describes something as “degenerate”—something that has fallen away from its proper condition or quality. It presents a condition rather than naming a person, place, or action. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jeremiah 2:21, so its normal meaning is established from a single recorded use rather than a broad range of passages. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding text.

gl: a hut (as of entwined boughs); also a lair
d: a hut (as of entwined boughs); also a lair

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a covert or covered place, while some renderings also use “also.” Its clearest supported sense is connected with shelter or concealment. It appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in three Psalms and once in Jeremiah. The word is used in passages involving a protected place or covering, including a den, pavilion, and covert. Its exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its normal sense points toward a concealed or sheltered place.

This Hebrew word refers to a named place, rendered “Sela.” It functions as a proper name rather than a general description of an object, person, or action. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both within 1 Samuel 23:28. Because the available wording identifies the place by name but does not provide a fuller definition, the safest meaning is simply the place name “Sela.” Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

gl: fault, iniquity, mischeif, punishment (of iniquity), sin.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “iniquity.” It is a noun used to speak of iniquity as something associated with a person or community, and it can be discussed in connection with bearing, confessing, or having it. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 232 times, showing that it is a well-established word for addressing iniquity across many kinds of passages. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

Azgad is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Azgad.” It identifies a group or individual associated with the returning exiles and the community recorded after the exile. The name appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezra and Nehemiah, and is consistently treated as a proper name rather than translated as an ordinary descriptive word. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding passage, but its normal function is to identify the person or family called Azgad.

gl: Unni , the name of two Israelites
d: Unni , the name of two Israelites

e.t: Unni is a personal name, identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs four times and is rendered “Unni.” Because names normally identify individuals instead of carrying a sentence-level definition, its basic meaning here is the person’s name. It appears in three verses, in passages from 1 Chronicles and Nehemiah. The surrounding verse is needed to identify which person named Unni is intended in a particular occurrence.

gl: a juniper (from its nudity of situation)
d: a juniper (from its nudity of situation)

e.t: This Hebrew word is a rare biblical term whose precise English meaning cannot be established from the available lexical information alone. It occurs only twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Jeremiah: 17:6 and 48:6. Because the verse text and an explicit definition are not available here, it would be misleading to assign a more specific meaning. Its exact sense must be determined from the wording and surrounding context of those passages.

gl: to dash in pieces, literally or figuratively (especially to disperse )
break (dash, shake) in (to) pieces, cast (abroad), disperse (selves), drive, retire, scatter (abroad), spread abroad.
d: to dash in pieces, literally or figuratively (especially to disperse )

e.t: This Hebrew word means “scattered,” describing people or things dispersed rather than remaining together. It can function as an action or description: people may be scattered across a land, a group may spread in different directions, or something may be distributed broadly. In the Old Testament, it occurs 68 times, so it expresses a recurring idea of separation and dispersion. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what is being scattered and the surrounding passage.

This word refers to judgment—the act or result of deciding a matter rightly. It names a judicial determination rather than describing a person, place, or action by itself. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 16:3, so its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. Its basic sense points to a decision concerning what is right or how a matter should be settled.

This Hebrew word refers to a “psaltery,” a musical instrument. It occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Daniel 3:5, 7, 10, and 15. Its role is that of a noun naming an instrument. The surrounding passage would be needed to explain how it functions in any one occurrence, but its basic meaning remains consistent across these four uses.

This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Isaiah 41:24, so its ordinary meaning cannot be established from repeated biblical usage. A careful reader should avoid assigning it a wider meaning than the surrounding verse supports. Its role is best understood by reading Isaiah 41:24 together with the surrounding lines, since the isolated word alone does not establish its full force.

This Hebrew word refers to an action associated with the grain offering in Leviticus 2:6, but its precise everyday meaning cannot be established from the available lexical information. It occurs only once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Leviticus 2:6. SEE relationships connect it with the offering and with other elements named in that verse, showing that it functions as part of the offering’s description. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its exact force there.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “high.” It functions as a descriptive term for something elevated or situated above the surrounding area. It appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in three verses, and its uses are connected with elevated places that people could occupy or use for refuge. The word’s basic sense remains focused on height rather than describing a person, action, or emotion. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word refers to something gathered or collected, but its exact everyday sense cannot be stated more precisely from the available lexical information. It occurs only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 57:13. In that verse, it functions as the object of verbs describing taking, carrying, possessing, and delivering, indicating that it names something people may seek to take hold of or depend on. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain its specific force there.

This Hebrew verb means “vomit”: to force something out from the stomach or body. It can describe a person vomiting, as in Job and Proverbs, and it can also portray land or a place rejecting its inhabitants. The word occurs eight times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages where the land is said to vomit out those who defile it. Its basic sense remains physical expulsion, whether the subject is a person or, figuratively, the land itself. Context determines what is being expelled.

gl: an Arvadite or citizen of Arvad
d: an Arvadite or citizen of Arvad

e.t: This Hebrew word identifies a person or people as an “Arvadite.” It functions as a group designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Genesis 10:18 and once in 1 Chronicles 1:16. The word’s normal sense is therefore an ethnic or family identification, while the surrounding verse supplies the particular role or setting in which the designation appears.

gl: to pour out (literally or figuratively), i.e. empty
× arm, cast out, draw (out), (make) empty, pour forth (out).
d: to pour out (literally or figuratively), i.e. empty

e.t: “Draw” is the supported meaning of this Hebrew verb. As an action word, it states what someone or something does in a sentence, connecting the subject with an object or result. This word appears 19 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across 19 verses, showing that it is used in more than one setting while retaining its central action sense. The surrounding sentence supplies the precise force in each occurrence.

Resen is a Hebrew proper name used for a place, not an ordinary descriptive word with a broader everyday meaning. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, and its English rendering is consistently “Resen.” Because no short definition or broader lexical gloss is provided, the safest understanding is simply the place-name itself. Its precise significance in Genesis 10:12 depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are handled separately from this word-level meaning.

gl: broidered (work), divers colours, (raiment of) needlework (on both sides).

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to decorative woven or embroidered work, especially material used for clothing or richly made fabric. It can describe garments, raiment, or other crafted textiles rather than a person or action. In its 12 Old Testament occurrences, it is associated with clothing and prepared materials, including garments presented or given. The central idea is fabric made with detailed workmanship, highlighting its crafted and ornamental character.

This Hebrew word refers to “blight,” a destructive condition affecting crops. It names a form of agricultural damage mentioned in six Old Testament verses, from Deuteronomy through Haggai. Scripture uses it among conditions that can bring loss upon fields and their produce. Its exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains blight affecting cultivated plants.

gl: properly, to vanquish ; by implication, to rule (causatively, crown)
make princes, have power, reign. See 5493 .
d: properly, to vanquish ; by implication, to rule (causatively, crown)

e.t: This Hebrew verb means “reigned.” It describes what a king or ruler did when exercising authority over a kingdom or people. The word appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, including Judges 9:22 and Hosea 12:4. Its verbal function presents ruling as an action carried out by a person, rather than as a title or place. The precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

The word means “tabernacle” and functions as a noun naming such a dwelling place. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Lamentations 2:6. The word’s precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical sense is a tabernacle. This term should therefore be understood as referring to the tabernacle itself rather than as an action, quality, or description.

Shiloah is a Hebrew proper name, referring to a specific place or feature rather than expressing a general action or quality. In English Bible renderings, it appears as “Shiloah.” The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Nehemiah 3:15 and Isaiah 8:6. Because it functions as a name, its basic meaning is identifying rather than describing; the precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

Shinab is a Hebrew personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Genesis 14:2, and is rendered “Shinab.” Because it functions as a name, its meaning is primarily identifying: it distinguishes one person from others mentioned in the biblical account. The surrounding verse and passage provide the details about that person, while the name itself does not describe a general concept.

This Hebrew word refers to a “casement,” a building opening associated with looking outward. It occurs twice in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, once in Judges 5:28 and once in Proverbs 7:6. Its use names a physical architectural feature rather than an action, person, or abstract idea. The precise force of the word in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary sense is a casement or window opening.

Shashai is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, in Ezra 10:40, and English translations retain it as “Shashai.” Because the available passage information does not include the verse text or a defined lexical meaning, the name itself is the clearest supported sense. Its significance in that passage must be understood from the surrounding account.

Tidal is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Tidal,” rather than an ordinary word describing an action or quality. It identifies a named person in Genesis 14, appearing twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Genesis 14:1 and 14:9. No explicit definition is given for the name, so its meaning here is its identifying function: Tidal names a person. Its significance in either verse must be understood from the surrounding passage, not from a separate word-definition.

This Hebrew noun refers to a garment—something worn as clothing, rendered “garment” in its one Old Testament occurrence. It names an article of clothing rather than an action, quality, or person. The word appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Esther 8:15. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is a garment or robe worn by someone.

e.t: This Hebrew word describes something “untempered”—something lacking the proper preparation needed to make it sound or reliable. In its seven Old Testament occurrences, it appears most often in Ezekiel, where it is connected with speech and with what people build or apply. The word therefore carries the idea of something presented as acceptable or protective but lacking the proper substance or preparation. Its precise force in any individual passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This rare Hebrew word is connected with a “night” that has “passed.” It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Daniel 6:18, and describes the passing of a night rather than naming a person, object, or enduring quality. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding Hebrew sentence, but its recorded sense centers on the night and its passing. This helps readers recognize it as a time-related expression with a completed action.
